title: MA9-10268
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the principal claimant) and his son XXXXX XXXXX XX XX XXXXXX (the claimant), both citizens of Mexico, are claiming protection in Canada because they allege that they would be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to their lives, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to their country. They are alleging that they are "persons in need of protection" under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).

The principal claimant alleges that his life was threatened by members of the union committee that he was a member of, because he had reported the fact that they had only become members for their own self-interest.

The principal claimant, on whom the refugee protection claim is based, basically alleges the following facts. He was a XXXXXXXXXXXX at a large company when he lost his job in XXXXXX 2000. After being unemployed for two years, a friend helped him to find work as an XXXXXX Mexico's XXXXX. He worked as an XXXX on call and, at the same time, as a XXXXXX XXXX XXXXX. At the end of 2008, the claimant was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX a committee to improve workers' rights. XXXX XXXXX was the XXXX of the committee that the claimant and XXXX other people sat on. The claimant made a list of the XXXX demands regarding the overtime hours they were not paid, the meals that were not included and the lack of cleanliness at work locations, among other things. The claimant brought the XXXX demands to the union committee. The committee members were not interested in them. Annoyed by the claimant, XXXX XXXXX even suggested that he leave his position on the union committee and return to working as an XXXX instead of harassing them with his demands. The claimant started receiving threatening telephone calls at his mother's house, where he was living. He had to change the telephone number. The threatening telephone calls continued on his son's cellphone. XXXX XXXXX physically attacked the claimant, punching him in the stomach, and pointed a gun at his head. A few days later, XXXX XXXXX hit claimant XXXXX in the face as he was leaving school. Another day, as they were leaving XXXXX, XXXXX was waiting for them in the parking lot and pointed his gun at them. The claimant received newspaper clippings about kidnappings that were meant to scare him. The claimant then decided to file a complaint against XXXX XXXXX with the public ministry. Four days later, he purchased airplane tickets because he decided to come and claim protection in Canada with his son, as his sister had done a few years before.
The claimants arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009, and claimed refugee protection that same day.
The panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection" for the following reasons. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimants entered Canada with their Mexican passports,1 which were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC). The panel is satisfied and finds that their identity has been established in accordance with section 106 of the IRPA. Credibility

The claimants have not credibly established the essential elements of their refugee protection claims. The claimant has not credibly established that he was a member of a union committee, which is the central element of his refugee protection claim. He has not credibly established that he made demands regarding the XXXX rights. He has not credibly established that he received death threats from XXXX XXXXX. The claimant's behaviour is inconsistent with his alleged fear.

The claimant was not a credible witness. The panel confronted the claimant about the fact that his narrative does not contain any dates and it therefore does not pinpoint when the events took place. When confronted by the panel, the claimant answered that he was nervous when he wrote his narrative and that he did not want to make any mistakes. He therefore chose to write a vague narrative. The panel is not satisfied with that answer because, if the events had really happened just before he arrived in Canada, it is reasonable to believe that he would not have had any problems in providing the months and years when the main alleged events occurred. Moreover, that narrative is very simple and quite short. Despite that, the claimant's testimony was often inconsistent or illogical. The claimant did not answer the panel's questions directly and he was unable to give clear answers to simple questions about his work as an XXXX.

The panel notes, first, that the claimants' alleged narrative has no relation to any of the grounds set out in section 96 of the IRPA. They are therefore not "refugees" within the meaning of section 96. Their fear is related to criminality and their claims should therefore be analyzed under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, since the claimants allege that they fear for their lives and are "persons in need of protection."

The claimant testified that he worked as an XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX from 2000 until his departure from Mexico in XXXX 2009. However, he stated under question 7, regarding his work experience, that he started in that position in XXXXX 2002. The claimant had a lot of trouble describing his work XXXXXXX; he wrote under question 7 that he was a XXXXXXXXX. After a number of questions to get him to clearly explain the nature of his work, the claimant stated that when people were needed for a XXXXXXXX, he had to XXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant testified that XXXX worked on call. Sometimes, he was working and other times not at all-it all depended on the XXXXX and the need. He testified that he was also a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX because his income was modest.

The claimant submitted into evidence under P-72 a card from XXXXX (XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX), which indicates that he was an XXXX and a XXXXXXXX. He has therefore credibly established that he worked in that field. He also established that he was a union member.

The panel asked the claimant whether he had any evidence establishing the principal facts alleged in support of his refugee protection claim-that he was a member of the union committee to defend workers' rights, a position that he alleges he was elected to. The claimant also alleged that he presented demands to the union committee, to the employer, and to the XXXXXX. The panel asked him whether he had any evidence establishing that he had presented those demands for the XXXX. The claimant answered that the union committee did everything verbally. Confronted by the panel with the fact that, when unions submit demands to employers, they normally do so in writing so that the employer can study them, the claimant changed his version of the facts. He added that there were indeed memos and letters regarding his demands, but that he had nothing. The claimant has no evidence establishing that he was a member of the union committee, or that he took any steps to defend the XXXX rights, which is supposedly what gave rise to his alleged persecution.

In Soto,3 Justice Boivin recalled, on March 23, 2011, that the refugee protection claimant bears the burden of proof. Justice Boivin stated the following: [25] The Court also agrees with the respondent's argument that the panel could have drawn a negative inference with respect to the applicant's credibility based on the fact that he did not give a reasonable explanation for his failure to submit evidence corroborating his allegations (Sinnathamby v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 473, [2001] F.C.J. No. 742, at paragraph 24). The Court already relied on this principle in Sosa, above, at paragraph 19, a case that contains facts similar to those in this case: [19] Last, this Court has also repeatedly confirmed that the RPD can draw an adverse inference from the lack of evidence corroborating a claimant's testimony where the panel has concerns about his or her credibility. The applicants had to properly document their alleged fear of persecution. In this case, the applicant did not provide any evidence to corroborate her place of residence during the period of alleged risk and did not even specify in her PIF where she lived during that period. It was therefore not unreasonable for the RPD to expect the applicants to provide credible evidence to corroborate the allegations that were at the heart of their claim and were the very foundation of their fear of persecution, given that the onus was on them to credibly establish their allegations in support of that fear, which they failed to do in this case.

The claimant alleged in his narrative that, at one point after he had threatened him verbally and over the telephone a number of times, XXXX XXXXX, the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX that the claimant was a member of, had attacked him by punching him in the stomach. He allegedly also pointed at gun to his head and told him that if he did not leave the committee, he would kill him and his son.

The panel asked the claimant whether he notified the union's executive council, his employer (XXXXXXXXXXX), or the police about these serious death threats. The claimant answered that he did not notify the police because he did not trust them and XXXXX had told him not to do so. He stated that he made an appointment with the union executive council and the employer, explaining the problem, and that they both apparently refused to receive the claimant and did not follow up on his written requests.

The claimant testified that, a few days later, his son was hit in the face by XXXXX, who gave him a threatening note for him. The claimant did not have the note to enter it on the record. The panel asked him whether he went to the police because, clearly, XXXX XXXXX, a violent and armed man who went to attack his son in the schoolyard, according to the alleged narrative, wanted to harm him. The claimant answered that he did nothing. The claimant explained that he did not go to the police because he thought that things would work out and that he wanted to defend the XXXXX rights. The panel confronted him with the fact that he had just testified that neither the union's executive council, nor the employer, nor the producers, nor his fellow XXXXX -who told him that they would go to work anyway, even if working conditions were difficult-supported him. The panel asked him how he could have thought that things would work out, given that he was the only one willing to fight for better working conditions, according to the alleged narrative. The claimant stated that he did not want to give up. The explanations for not having requested protection from the police are illogical and inconsistent, since, according to what he alleged, the situation was not going to improve.

It is reasonable to believe that if the claimant and his son had received death threats daily by telephone and XXXXX had already pointed a gun at them, the claimant would have taken measures to protect himself by ending his participation on the committee. Furthermore, the panel asked him why he did not find another sales clerk job in a boutique or café, if he had so many enemies in XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant answered that jobs are scarce and that, in Mexico, at the age of 47, he was considered too old to receive job offers. Even if the claimant had credibly established the facts alleged in his narrative, which is not the case, he still would not have established his well-founded fear of persecution.

In Liberato,4 Justice Mactavish recalled that a person must take the measures available to protect himself before seeking international protection, such as quitting a job that could be dangerous, for example. Justice Mactavish recalled that the Federal Court had stated that principle more than 10 years prior; she stated the following: [28] In Sanchez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 99, the Federal Court of Appeal considered the extent to which a claimant should be expected to make choices to free him- or herself from the risk of harm, before being able to seek international protection. In this regard, the Court concluded that it was not unreasonable to expect an individual to take steps to protect themselves that would not deprive the individual of a general ability to earn a living. There is no evidence in this case that Mr. Liberato would not be able to find another job in Mexico City.

The claimant submitted into evidence under P-4 two medical certificates-strangely, they are from the same surgeon-regarding the two minor assaults against him and his son. By chance, the claimants were allegedly treated by the same surgeon at the hospital some 10 days apart.

Given that the claimant has not established that he was a member of the union committee and that his alleged behaviour is inconsistent with that of a person who claims his life was threatened daily, but who continued to attend to his business as usual by living at the same house until he left Mexico, the panel gives no probative value to these documents submitted as P-4.

The claimant justified his unwillingness to file a complaint with the police following the death threats that he allegedly received and the attacks of XXXX 2009 and XXX 2009 by the fact that he does not trust the police in Mexico. Confronted with the fact that a few days before he left Mexico, on XXXXX, 2009, he filed a complaint anyway, the claimant answered that he wanted to obtain protection. Yet if the claimant really wanted the police to help, it is reasonable to believe that he would have gone to them as soon as the alleged death threats had begun in 2008. The claimant would not have purchased an airplane ticket four days later on XXXXX, 2009,1 leaving the police investigators no opportunity to do their work. The panel is of the opinion that that complaint was merely for convenience, in order to bolster his refugee protection claim.

The claimants have not credibly established the facts alleged in support of their narrative. They are neither "refugees under section 96 of the IRPA" nor "persons in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel determines that the claimants have not satisfactorily discharged their burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility that they will be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to their country.

For these reasons, the refugee protection claims filed by XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and his son, XXXXX XXXXX XX XX XXXXXX, are rejected.
